---
title: "Exercise 3.9"
---

## Solution
First, we consider the case where $m$ and $n$ are finite.

Let
$$ \mathcal A = \{ A \in \mathcal B : m(A) = n(A) \}.$$
We will show that $\mathcal A$ is a monotone class. 

1. If $A_i \uparrow A$ and each $A_i \in \mathcal A$, then
    \begin{align*}
        m(A) = m\left(\bigcup_i A_i \right) &= m \left(A_1 \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} (A_{i+1}-A_{i}) \right)
        = m(A_1)+ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}m(A_{i+1}-A_{i}) \\
        &= m(A_1)+ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\big( m(A_{i+1})-m(A_{i}) \big)
        = n(A_1)+ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\big( n(A_{i+1})-n(A_{i}) \big) \\
    & = n \left(A_1 \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} (A_{i+1}-A_{i}) \right) = n\left(\bigcup_i A_i \right) \\[5pt]
    &= n(A).
    \end{align*}

    Hence, $A \in \mathcal A$. 

2. Suppose that $A_i \downarrow A$ and each $A_i \in \mathcal A$. 
    Since
    $$(-i,i)\uparrow\mathbb R,$$
    we have $\mathbb R \in \mathcal A$. Thus, if $E\in\mathcal A$, then
    $$m(E^c)=m(\mathbb R)-m(E)=n(\mathbb R)-n(E)=n(E^c),$$
    which implies that $E^c\in\mathcal A$.
    Thus, we have $A_i^c \in \mathcal A$.

    Since $A_i^c\uparrow A^c$, Step 1 implies that $A^c\in\mathcal A$.
    Thus, we have $A\in\mathcal A$.

Therefore, $\mathcal A$ is a monotone class.

<br>

Next, we will show that $\mathcal B = \mathcal A$.


Let $\mathcal C$ be the collection of all finite disjoint unions of intervals of the forms
$$(a,b],\qquad (-\infty,b],\qquad (a,\infty),$$
where $a,b\in\mathbb R$, together with $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb R$. 
Then $\mathcal C$ is an algebra and
$$\sigma(\mathcal C)=\mathcal B.$$

First, for any $a<b$, we have
$$(a,b+1/n)\downarrow(a,b].$$
Since each $(a,b+1/n)\in\mathcal A$ by assumption and $\mathcal A$ is a monotone class, 
it follows that
$$(a,b]\in\mathcal A.$$
Next, for any $b\in\mathbb R$,
$$(-n,b]\uparrow(-\infty,b].$$

Since $(-n,b]\in\mathcal A$ for all sufficiently large $n$, 
the monotone class property gives
$$(-\infty,b]\in\mathcal A.$$

We know that $\mathcal A$ is closed under complements.
Hence
$$(a,\infty)=(-\infty,a]^c\in\mathcal A.$$

Therefore, $m$ and $n$ agree on every interval used in the definition of $\mathcal C$. 
By finite additivity, they agree on every finite disjoint union of such intervals. Hence,
$$\mathcal C\subset\mathcal A.$$

Since $\mathcal A$ is a monotone class containing $\mathcal C$,
$$\mathcal M(\mathcal C)\subset\mathcal A.$$
By the monotone class theorem,
$$\mathcal B=\sigma(\mathcal C)=\mathcal M(\mathcal C),$$
and therefore
$$\mathcal B\subset\mathcal A.$$
Since $\mathcal A\subset\mathcal B$ by definition, we conclude that
$$\mathcal A=\mathcal B.$$
Thus,
$$m(A)=n(A) \qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal B.$$


<br>

Now suppose that at least one of $m$ and $n$ is not finite.
For $k \in \mathbb N$, define
$$ m_k(A) = m(A \cap (-k,k)), \quad n_k(A) = n(A \cap (-k,k)).$$
Thus $m_k$ and $n_k$ are finite, since
$$ m((-k,k)) = n((-k,k)) <\infty.$$

For any open interval $(a,b)$, we know that $(a,b) \cap (-k,k)$ is an open interval or the emptyset. Thus,
$$ m_k((a,b)) = m((a,b)\cap(-k,k)) = n((a,b)\cap(-k,k)) = n_k(a,b).$$
Hence, from finite case, we can say that $m_k(A)=n_k(A)$ for any $A \in \mathcal B$.

For any $A \in \mathcal B$, defined
$$A_k = A \cap (-k,k).$$
Then we have
$$ A_k \uparrow A.$$
Since
$$ m(A_k)=n(A_k) $$
for every $k$, and
$$ A = A_1 \cup \bigcup_{k=2}^{\infty}(A_k\setminus A_{k-1}),$$
we obtain
$$ m(A) = m(A_1) + \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} m(A_k\setminus A_{k-1}) = n(A_1) + \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} n(A_k\setminus A_{k-1})= n(A).$$
